items.title: Demographics often predict less than marketers assume
items.claim: Mark Ritson and others have argued that traditional demographic segmentation (age, income, gender) often performs poorly. What's the evidence?

options.text: Demographics predict purchase behaviour with high accuracy
Within-group variation in purchase behaviour is often larger than between-group variation; behavioural segmentation (what people actually buy) typically outperforms demographic segmentation
Demographics are legally required for marketing
Segmentation has been abandoned in modern marketing

items.reveal:
Byron Sharp's 'How Brands Grow' (2010), drawing on the Ehrenberg-Bass Institute, argued that mass-market brands grow through reach, not narrow targeting — and that demographic targeting often misallocates spend. Coca-Cola buyers, Toyota buyers and HSBC customers look broadly similar demographically.

Behavioural segmentation (heavy vs light buyers, lapsed vs active) typically explains more variance. Geographic and psychographic add incremental power.
items.why: Marketing teaching often defaults to demographic segmentation because it's easy to teach and the data is available. The evidence suggests it's a weaker guide than is taught.

items.title: Quality assurance and quality control are different things
items.claim: A car plant inspects every vehicle at the end of the line and rejects defective units. Which approach is this?

options.text: Quality assurance, because it ensures quality
Quality control — defect detection after the fact. Quality assurance builds quality into the process so defects don't arise

items.reveal:
W. Edwards Deming, who worked in postwar Japan, argued that inspecting defects out is more expensive than preventing them. His '14 Points' for management (1986) included 'cease dependence on inspection to achieve quality'.

Toyota's andon-cord system stops the line whenever a worker sees a problem — quality is built upstream. Quality control still happens, but as a back-stop, not the main mechanism. ISO 9001 audits processes (assurance), not products (control).
items.why: Two firms with identical defect rates can have very different cost structures depending on whether defects are prevented or caught.

items.title: PESTLE is a checklist, not a model
items.claim: PESTLE analysis covers Political, Economic, Social, Technological, Legal and Environmental factors. What is its main analytical limitation?

options.text: It can predict the future with high accuracy
It generates an inventory of factors but does not weight them, link them or model their interactions — students often produce long unprioritised lists
It is legally required for UK firms
It only applies to large firms

items.reveal_title: A scanning tool, not a strategy
items.reveal:
PESTLE (originally PEST, expanded over time) traces to Francis Aguilar's 'Scanning the Business Environment' (1967). It's a structured way to spot environmental change but provides no mechanism to prioritise or combine factors.

Scenario planning (Royal Dutch Shell, from Pierre Wack in the 1970s) goes further: it builds plausible coherent futures and tests strategy against them. PESTLE feeds into scenario planning, not the other way around.
items.why: PESTLE is useful for ensuring you haven't missed an external factor. It's not a strategy tool on its own.
